Model Predictive Path Integral Control as
Preconditioned Gradient Descent
Mahyar Fazlyab, Sina Sharifi, Jiarui Wang
Abstract—Abstract— Model Predictive Path Integral
(MPPI) control is a popular sampling-based method for tra-
jectory optimization in nonlinear and nonconvex settings,
yet its optimization structure remains only partially un-
derstood. We develop a variational, optimization-theoretic
interpretation of MPPI by lifting constrained trajectory op-
timization to a KL-regularized problem over distributions
and reducing it to a negative log-partition (free-energy)
objective over a tractable sampling family. For a general
parametric family, this yields a preconditioned gradient
method on the distribution parameters and a natural multi-
step extension of MPPI. For the fixed-covariance Gaussian
family, we show that classical MPPI is recovered exactly as
a preconditioned gradient descent step with unit step size.
This interpretation enables a direct convergence analysis:
under bounded feasible sets, we derive an explicit upper
bound on the smoothness constant and a simple sufficient
condition guaranteeing descent of exact MPPI. Numerical
experiments support the theory and illustrate the effect of
key hyperparameters on performance.
Index Terms— Optimal control, Optimization Algorithms,
Predictive control for nonlinear systems
I. INTRODUCTION
Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, e.g., [13,
15], is a widely used sampling-based method for trajectory
optimization in nonlinear and nonconvex settings, owing to
its simplicity, parallelizability, and ability to handle nondif-
ferentiable dynamics and costs. In its standard form, MPPI
updates the sampling distribution by drawing perturbed control
sequences, reweighting them according to their trajectory
costs, and shifting the nominal control toward a weighted
average of the sampled rollouts. Despite its empirical success
in robotics and real-time control, this update is typically
introduced through stochastic optimal control or control-as-
inference arguments, which do not directly expose its underly-
ing optimization structure. As a result, basic questions such as
how MPPI relates to gradient-based methods, when its update
is guaranteed to decrease a well-defined objective, and how
its hyperparameters influence stability and convergence remain
only partially understood [4]. These gaps motivate the need for
a direct optimization-theoretic interpretation of MPPI.

{mahyarfazlyab, sshari12, jwang486}@jhu.eduA. Contributions
This paper provides a variational, optimization-theoretic
foundation for MPPI by reinterpreting it asstochastic opti-
mization of a negative log-partition (free-energy) objective.
We lift constrained trajectory optimization to a KL-regularized
problem over distributions and show that it reduces to min-
imizing a free-energy objective over a tractable sampling
family. For a general parametric family, we derive exact
gradient and Hessian formulas for the reduced objective and
obtain a preconditioned gradient method on the parameters
of the sampling distribution, leading naturally to a multi-step
extension of MPPI. For the fixed-covariance Gaussian family,
we then show that classical MPPI is recovered exactly as
a preconditioned gradient descent step with unit step size.
This interpretation enables a direct convergence analysis; in
particular, under bounded feasible sets, we derive an explicit
upper bound on the smoothness constant and a simple suf-
ficient condition guaranteeing descent of exact MPPI with
unit step size. Finally, we support the theory with numerical
experiments on two trajectory optimization benchmarks: a
linear–quadratic regulator (LQR) problem and a Dubins car
navigating a cluttered environment. While our emphasis is
on trajectory optimization, the development is modular and
applies more broadly to constrained sampling-based optimiza-
tion.
B. Related Work
Probabilistic Inference Perspective:Inference-based formu-
lations recast control as posterior inference over action se-
quences conditioned on an optimality variable, leading to
updates closely related to MPPI [4]. This viewpoint has been
developed extensively in reinforcement learning and control
[6], and extended to model predictive control via variational
inference [10]. In particular, [10] introduced a variational
inference MPC framework that recovers several sampling-
based optimization methods, including MPPI [14], CEM [1],
and CMA-ES [2] as special cases. Our contribution is com-
plementary: rather than deriving MPPI through inference, we
show that it can be obtained directly as a preconditioned
gradient step on a KL-regularized free-energy objective.
Diffusion Perspective:Another line of work connects MPPI
to model-based diffusion [11, 16, 5]. In [16], building on the
score estimation result from [11], that MPPI can be interpreted
as performing score ascent on a Gaussian-smoothed Gibbs
distribution. Although this interpretation explains the mecha-
nism of MPPI, it still does not directly reveal its convergencearXiv:2603.24489v1  [math.OC]  25 Mar 2026

properties.
Optimization Perspective:MPPI has also been related to
optimization-based updates. For example, [7] showed that
path integral policy improvement [12] can be viewed as
mirror descent (MD) over trajectory distributions, where each
update minimizes an expected cost regularized by a KL
divergence and leads to exponential reweighting. Building on
this perspective, [9] proposed momentum and adaptive step-
size mechanisms to accelerate convergence. In practice, these
MD updates must be projected onto a parametric family to
retain tractable sampling and preserve the structure of the
distribution. For Gaussian families, the resulting algorithm
recovers standard MPPI.
Theoretical Analysis of MPPI:Motivated by the empirical
success of MPPI, several recent works have begun to study its
theoretical properties. In particular, CoVO-MPC[17] analyzes
the convergence behavior of MPPI using contraction theory,
proving at least linear convergence for (time-varying) LQR.
However, the contraction result cannot be extended to general
nonlinear settings without making extra regularity assump-
tions. Separately, [3] studies the optimality and suboptimality
of MPPI in stochastic and deterministic settings, with an
emphasis on deterministic MPPI and its approximation error.
Our analysis is complementary to these works: we analyze
the convergence for general nonlinear systems and cost, with
bounded feasible set being the main requirement.

VI. CONCLUSION
This paper showed that MPPI admits a direct variational and
optimization-theoretic interpretation. By lifting constrained
trajectory optimization to a KL-regularized problem over
distributions, we obtained a free-energy objective whose opti-
mization over a parametric sampling family yields a precon-
ditioned gradient method. In the Gaussian fixed-covariance
setting, this recovers classical MPPI exactly and leads to
explicit descent and stationarity guarantees, as well as a simple
covariance-dependent design rule for unit-step MPPI. These
results help demystify MPPI from an optimization viewpoint
and open the door to principled extensions of sampling-based
control methods.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary: This partial document introduces a new optimization-theoretic interpretation of Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, a popular sampling-based method for trajectory optimization. The authors reframe MPPI as a preconditioned gradient descent method applied to a negative log-partition (free-energy) objective. They show that for a general parametric family of distributions, MPPI corresponds to a preconditioned gradient method on the distribution parameters, leading to a multi-step extension. Specifically for the fixed-covariance Gaussian family, they demonstrate that classical MPPI is equivalent to a preconditioned gradient descent step with a unit step size. This interpretation allows for a direct convergence analysis, providing an upper bound on the smoothness constant and a condition for descent under bounded feasible sets. The paper also discusses related work from probabilistic inference and diffusion perspectives, highlighting how their contribution complements existing interpretations by directly linking MPPI to gradient-based optimization. Numerical experiments are presented to support the theoretical findings.

nodes.title: Diffusion Perspective
nodes.summary:
This document presents a new interpretation of Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, a popular sampling-based method for trajectory optimization. The authors reframe MPPI as a preconditioned gradient descent method operating on the parameters of a sampling distribution. They achieve this by:

1.  **Variational Formulation:** Lifting the constrained trajectory optimization problem to a KL-regularized problem over probability distributions.
2.  **Free-Energy Objective:** Reducing this problem to minimizing a negative log-partition (free-energy) objective over a tractable sampling family.
3.  **Preconditioned Gradient Descent:** Demonstrating that for a general parametric family, this leads to a preconditioned gradient method on the distribution parameters.
4.  **MPPI Recovery:** Showing that for the specific case of fixed-covariance Gaussian distributions, classical MPPI is recovered exactly as a preconditioned gradient descent step with a unit step size.
5.  **Convergence Analysis:** This new interpretation enables a direct convergence analysis, providing an explicit upper bound on the smoothness constant and a sufficient condition for MPPI's descent under bounded feasible sets.

The paper also discusses related work from probabilistic inference, diffusion, and optimization perspectives, highlighting how their contribution complements existing understanding by directly linking MPPI to gradient-based optimization. Numerical experiments on LQR and a Dubins car problem are used to support the theoretical findings.

nodes.title: Optimization Perspective
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the optimization perspective and theoretical analysis of MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral control). It highlights MPPI's connection to optimization-based updates, specifically mirror descent, and how momentum and adaptive step-size mechanisms can accelerate convergence. The document also reviews existing theoretical analyses of MPPI, including convergence proofs for LQR and studies on optimality and suboptimality in stochastic and deterministic settings. It then introduces a variational formulation for trajectory optimization as a constrained minimization problem. This formulation is lifted to an optimization problem over probability distributions, leading to a KL-regularized distributional problem. The core idea is to optimize a base distribution within a tractable family to obtain the tightest upper bound on the original constrained problem, ultimately reducing to minimizing the negative log-partition function. The document also defines notation used throughout the text.

nodes.title: Optimizing the Base Distribution
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses the optimization perspective and theoretical analysis of MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral). It highlights MPPI's connection to optimization-based updates, specifically mirror descent, and how momentum and adaptive step-size mechanisms can accelerate convergence. The document also reviews existing theoretical analyses of MPPI, noting their limitations in general nonlinear settings and contrasting them with the current work's focus on convergence for general nonlinear systems with bounded feasible sets.

The document then introduces a variational formulation for trajectory optimization as a constrained minimization problem. It proposes lifting this problem to an optimization over probability distributions, leading to a KL-regularized distributional formulation. This formulation involves trading off expected cost with proximity to a base distribution. The core idea is to optimize the base distribution within a tractable family (e.g., Gaussians) to obtain a principled approach for optimizing the sampling distribution.

The document details the process of optimizing over a parametric sampling family, deriving expressions for the gradient and Hessian of the reduced objective function. It then presents a preconditioned gradient descent method for minimizing this objective, outlining how to approximate the gradient using sampled importance weights. Finally, it provides a convergence analysis for the preconditioned gradient iteration, establishing conditions for descent, summability of gradients, and stationarity.

The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Reformulation:** The original problem is reduced to minimizing a function $F(\theta)$ which depends on the parameter $\theta$ of the sampling distribution. This reduced problem is expressed as $F(\theta) = -\tau \log Z(\theta)$.
*   **Assumptions for Differentiability:** Assumption 1 is introduced to ensure that the reduced objective function $F(\theta)$ is twice continuously differentiable with respect to $\theta$, allowing for gradient-based optimization.
*   **Preconditioned Gradient Descent:** The document proposes using a preconditioned gradient descent method to minimize $F(\theta)$. This approach leverages the differentiability of $F(\theta)$ with respect to the distribution parameters.
*   **Gradient and Hessian Expressions:** Lemma 1 provides explicit formulas for the gradient ($\nabla F(\theta)$) and Hessian ($\nabla^2 F(\theta)$) of the reduced objective function. These expressions are crucial for designing and analyzing gradient-based algorithms.
*   **Sampling-Based Gradient Estimation:** Since the exact expectation in the gradient calculation is often intractable, the document outlines a method to estimate the gradient using samples drawn from the current distribution $\pi_{\theta_k}$. This involves using self-normalized importance weights.
*   **Algorithm 1: Multi-step MPPI:** A specific algorithm, "Multi-step MPPI," is presented, detailing the steps for sampling, approximating the gradient, and updating the parameters $\theta$ over multiple iterations.
*   **Convergence Analysis:** Lemma 2 and Theorem 1 provide a convergence analysis for the preconditioned gradient descent iteration. They establish conditions (Assumption 2 and a step size constraint) under which the algorithm guarantees descent, summability of preconditioned gradients, and stationarity.

structure.title: CONCLUSION
structure.summary: The provided document excerpt concludes with a section on the paper's findings and an appendix containing mathematical proofs. The conclusion highlights that Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control can be interpreted through a variational and optimization-theoretic lens. The paper demonstrates that by reformulating constrained trajectory optimization as a KL-regularized problem over distributions, a free-energy objective is derived. Optimizing this objective over a parametric sampling family leads to a preconditioned gradient method. In the specific case of Gaussian distributions with fixed covariance, this approach precisely recovers classical MPPI and provides explicit guarantees for descent and stationarity, along with a simple covariance-dependent design rule for unit-step MPPI. These contributions aim to clarify MPPI from an optimization perspective and pave the way for principled extensions of sampling-based control methods. The appendix provides detailed proofs for Lemma 1 and Lemma 2, involving differentiation of objective functions and Hessian computations, as well as Taylor expansions and bounding techniques. A list of references is also included, citing related works in optimization, reinforcement learning, and control.
